1:
What kind of thing the following chapters are is settled three ways before anything is expounded. Gill says simply that the book begins here with the first sermon, the preceding chapter being only a preface. Keil and Delitzsch compare the six longer discourses with the shorter sayings gathered later: those carry headings giving date and circumstances, these give none, and the six read not like addresses delivered to the people but like treatises compiled in writing out of the prophet's oral preaching. Ellicott offers a third account from the book's own history, that since the record of the work under the first reign was destroyed by the next king and re-written from memory, what we have is probably a precis of the burnt roll, with some additions and possibly some omissions.

Henry makes the sending itself a lesson. The man had a general charge already and here receives a particular one, which is good for ministers, who should by faith and prayer take out a fresh commission and compare what they carry with the word, so as to say not only that the Lord sent them but that he sent them to speak this. And he marks the change of address: out of a pleasant retirement among a few friends and the study of the law, into a noisy tumultuous city, to cry in the ears of people who had stopped their ears.

Whose kindness is remembered divides them. Clarke says flatly that it was the kindness God showed in taking them to be his people, and not theirs to him, and Calvin agrees, since God regarded nothing they deserved and ascribed his care of them to his own former benefits. Ellicott reads the opposite: the verse contrasts the faithfulness of the past with the unfaithfulness of the present, the bride ready to follow her lord into an unsown land. Wesley splits the difference and makes it mutual, a reminder of the kindness that was between them.

The two terms they date alike. Clarke takes the youth for their infant political state at the coming out of Egypt, when they just began to be a people, having had before neither constitution nor form of government, and the espousals for the receiving of the law, an acceptance compared to a betrothal. Ellicott puts the espousals at the same covenant and traces the marriage figure backwards and forwards, implied already in the jealous God of the law, worked out as history and parable by one earlier prophet, and expanded more fully by a later one.

Holiness unto the Lord they read off the priesthood. Gill lists what made it so: choice, covenant, holy laws, a sanctuary placed among them, and a high priest carrying those very words on the front of his mitre. Ellicott names the same gold plate and adds the term for a holy thing used of the consecrated gifts that fell to the priests, concluding that the nation itself had a priestly character and was consecrated as firstfruits of the harvest of the world. Clarke keeps the legal edge: they were as wholly the Lord's as the firstfruits were the priests' own property. Calvin will not let it be praise, since the title stands in implied contrast with the wickedness of a people who afterwards fell away from a God so liberal to them.

What happens to those who devour him is a question of one word. Clarke makes it trespass on divine property, so that they who persecute God's children have a grievous burden to bear and an awful account to give. Ellicott traces the verb through the law, where it covers transgressions against the ceremonial code, and prefers here to render it shall be condemned, or shall be made to suffer: the invaders and oppressors are guilty as of a sacrilege that will not go unpunished.
4:
Who is being summoned they take differently. Gill limits it to the two tribes and their families, the ten having long since gone into captivity, all being called because all were guilty; Keil and Delitzsch let it run against the whole people. Calvin reads the summons as a rhetorical move: by this preface God seeks attention, intimating no common subject, and the prophet comes forward fearing no defence that could disprove the justice of the reproof.

The question put to the fathers they answer by denying its premise. Gill asks what injustice could be alleged, since there is no unrighteousness in God, or what unfaithfulness, since no promise of his fails. Clarke turns it on the law and the government: had they discovered anything cruel or oppressive in the one, anything tyrannical in the other? Ellicott hears a wronged husband asking whether he has failed in anything, and takes vanity for a name of idol-worship. Calvin finds two crimes, that they departed from a God they had found to be a deliverer and became vain in their devices, the sin aggravated because no occasion had been given: vanity alone was the reason they went.

The wilderness is painted hard, and one of them qualifies the painting. Clarke makes it a country where the means of life were not to be found, where no single family could have subsisted, much less six hundred thousand men, so that their being fed at all was a special providence; it was the shadow of death in appearance, the grave to whoever committed himself to it. Keil and Delitzsch keep the benefits in view, the bringing out of the house of bondage and the leading through pathless deserts, reading the silence as taking no thought of one they owed everything to. Ellicott alone notes that the colours are laid on to heighten a contrast, and that the picture was true of part but not the whole of the region.

The plentiful country is a word they all stop at. Gill gives the Hebrew as a land of Carmel; Ellicott explains that the word means a vine-clad hill and had become a type of plenty, and that the Greek took it for a proper name; Calvin declines to turn the words in all directions; Keil and Delitzsch render it fruitful fields, the opposite of the wilderness.

What followed the entry they date at once. Ellicott points to the rapid degeneracy after the settlement, the false worship and foul crimes of the old chronicles, a nation meant to be the pattern and firstfruits of mankind sinking to the level of the heathen or below. Keil and Delitzsch explain why the land is called a heritage: the Lord of the whole earth possesses it, gave it to them, and yet dwells in the midst of it as its real lord, so that defiling it made his own domain an object of horror.

The failure of the guides is the heart of the charge. Ellicott says what weighed most on the prophets was that those called to guide were the chief agents in the evil, and adds that the rebuke came from the lips of a priest. On who the law-handlers were he and Clarke part: Clarke makes them expositors whose office is to draw out the law's spiritual meaning, Ellicott priests, since the order of non-priestly scribes does not appear until after the captivity. Clarke reads the pastors as kings and civil rulers; Ellicott prefers shepherds, the English word having grown too religious. Calvin turns the passage against a defence he expects: many think they hold a shield against God when they plead that they lacked learning to tell light from darkness and only followed their rulers, but the prophet does not cast the people's faults on the leaders, and from the least to the greatest they had rejected God and his law.
9:
What pleading means divides them. Clarke keeps it forensic: I will maintain my process, vindicate my conduct and prove the wickedness of yours. Ellicott hears the injured husband of an earlier prophet appearing as accuser, setting out the bride's guilt as an indictment. Gill allows either words or deeds, reproof or punishment. Henry makes pleading the alternative to punishment, since before God punishes he pleads to bring men to repentance, and adds that those who deal with sinners must urge a variety of arguments and follow their blow. Calvin gets the opposite from the word yet: let them not think they have already suffered all, for God keeps his right entire and will pursue it to their children's children, hypocrites being apt to cast off fear once chastised.

Where the prophet is sending them is disputed four ways. Gill takes Chittim from a son of Javan who held the island now called Cyprus, the Hebrews then extending the name to all islands and maritime places. Clarke reports the same island on the historian's authority, and a later book making it Macedonia, but prefers a scholar's case that the Chittim held Italy and the neighbouring European coast. Calvin says the Hebrews called the Greeks by the name, though thinking it belonged properly to the Macedonians, and treats the two names as Greece on one side and the East on the other, a part for the whole. Ellicott ignores the identification and takes the pair as furthest west and furthest east, so that the whole earth might be searched without finding a parallel.

The comparison itself they all feel. Clarke sharpens it: nations near or remote, cultivated or stupid, kept gods they owed nothing to, while these abandoned the God they owed life and breath to. Gill adds that traders carrying their gods from port to port and tent-dwellers moving from desert to desert kept them still, and passes on the Jewish report that one people worshipped water and the other fire, and that though the one god would quench the other neither would change; other writers, he notes, relate the two exactly the reverse. Calvin will not let the constancy be praise: God does not commend the nations for holding to their superstitions, though set beside his own people's conduct it might look laudable.

Whether the heavens are commanded or described is a question Clarke raises, the original admitting either. Ellicott glosses the verb in its old sense, thunder-stricken, and finds the adjuration already familiar from the older scriptures, the whole universe shocked at an offence against its Creator. Calvin explains the manoeuvre: prophets address heaven and earth, which have no understanding, and pass over men who have, doing it in hopeless cases where they find no disposition to learn; the thing is as though we saw heaven and earth mixed together.

The two evils are counted the same way and weighed differently. Clarke names them plainly, forsaking the fountain of life and light and hewing cisterns from idols that could yield neither temporal nor spiritual good, and presses the word broken to mean vessels ill made and not staunch, so that the water leaked away. Ellicott distinguishes the two waters, the one flowing from the rock and the other only a tank for surface water. Calvin measures the folly: to leave an old friend for a new one is base, but where there is no compensation it is folly, levity and madness together, for what is it but madness to despise what one knows to be profitable and embrace what will do harm?

Gill alone stops at whose evils they were: the aggravation is that the people of God committed them, and such may fall into great sins and yet remain his, since covenant interest cannot be dissolved, a thing he offers not as encouragement to sin but as relief under the sense of it.
14:
The opening question they answer by denying it, all but one. Gill takes the servant for one who no longer abides in his own house but is carried captive and used as a slave. Clarke asks whether he is a slave bought with money or a servant born in the family, and answers, a son. Henry piles up the reasons: they are children and heirs, the seed of God's friend and of his chosen, not the son of the bondwoman but of the free, designed for dominion and not servitude. Calvin says the same from their charter, free beyond all nations as the firstborn son of God, so that a new cause must be looked for. Ellicott alone reverses the sense: the word had become through an earlier prophet a term of honour rather than shame, and of all servants the one born in the house stood nearest a son, so that the question is not whether Israel has become a slave but why the household servant of Jehovah is treated as one with no master to protect him.

The lions divide the metaphorical from the literal. Gill makes them the kings of the nations on the Jewish commentators' authority, likened to lions for strength and cruelty, their roaring standing for armies brought out and the din of battle; Clarke names the Assyrians who sacked the northern kingdom. Calvin keeps the figure but adds contempt to cruelty, since it is more degrading when God lets men be torn by beasts, and notes that the prophet drops the metaphor and says plainly that the land was desolate. Ellicott takes the beasts at face value: lions had attacked, not figuratively only as symbols of invaders but in the most literal sense, and they had made the land waste.

The two Egyptian cities set them looking things up. Gill gives Noph as Memphis, once the palace of the kings and now the great city on the Nile, and takes the other for a capital and royal seat. Ellicott reports that the Greek translators made the first Memphis in the north while later critics prefer a city far to the south, and decides for the north because the second stood on the eastern mouth of the river and on the frontier.

Why Egypt appears at all is answered three ways. Keil and Delitzsch explain it from the prophet's own moment: as help had once been sought from that quarter against Assyria, so now it was being sought against the Chaldeans. Calvin reads the particle: not only professed enemies but the very friends they confided in would turn their power against them; and he declines the suggestion that the shame lies in being beaten by a people the old historians called unwarlike, since Scripture does not say it. Clarke supplies a date instead, the defeat and death of the good king in battle with the Egyptians, and calls that the breaking of the crown of the head. Ellicott stays with the verb, rendered shall feed on or depasture so as to produce baldness, a reproach and so a natural symbol of a people's ruin.

The cause is stated plainly and pressed hard. Gill says their idolatry and forsaking of God brought Egyptians and Babylonians alike on them. Calvin puts it as a sentence to be swallowed: thou hast concocted this evil for thyself, and the blame cannot be cast on God, who would have been faithful had impiety not prevented him.

What way he led them in is a flat contradiction. Keil and Delitzsch refuse to take it of the right way of life, because the clause fixes the leading within a definite time, while God leads his people rightly at all times; the way must be the particular road he brought them by. Ellicott says it is scarcely the literal path through the wilderness but much rather the true way of life.
18:
Both rivers stand for kingdoms, and two of them say so in nearly the same words. Clarke identifies the first as the Nile and insists that the second, called simply the river, always means the Euphrates, the land between it and the Tigris being called to this day the country beyond the river. Ellicott makes the principle explicit, that great rivers were in the poetry of the prophets the natural symbols of the kingdoms they flowed through; he glosses the first name as the turbid or muddy water, notes that elsewhere it stands not for the Nile but for the border stream between Palestine and Egypt, and observes that the second needed no name at all, being pre-eminent in greatness.

What the two errands were is filled in from the histories. Gill allows either an imitation of Egyptian idols or the sending of ambassadors for help, when they had their God so near, and gives two instances of the second kind: a king who had no business marching against the Egyptian, and a remnant who went down into Egypt against an express word. Clarke says they made alliances with two nations that were always jealous of them and sought their ruin, the one a broken reed instead of a staff and the other a leaky cistern. Ellicott shows the policy was old: two kings had courted Assyria, one Babylon, and another had sought Egyptian help, while an earlier prophet rebuked both courses; even under the reforming reign there was an Egyptian party, and under the two kings before it that party was in power, the name of one of them probably bearing witness to the fact.

Calvin turns the two errands into an image of aggravated sin. Their misery could not be laid at any door but their own, and the guilt was doubled because, instead of the one remedy of reconciliation with God, they looked here and there for vain ones and so heaped up new causes of misery. Suppose a sick man who knows the cause of his disease and, passing by what would cure him, has recourse to expedients that injure his recovery: is he not held worthy to die, for despising what might have healed him and indulging himself in what is deceptive?

How wickedness corrects is where they divide. Gill offers two constructions, that the ill success of the errands to Egypt and Assyria was itself an instruction correcting their folly, or that their wickedness was a just reason why the Lord chastened them; Wesley keeps the second, that their own wickedness is the cause of their correction, and adds that they need only consider to be convinced. Ellicott and Calvin make the sin itself the executioner. Ellicott says the strain rises here from what is local and temporary to the eternal law of retribution, punishment coming as the natural consequence of sin and our pleasant vices becoming whips to scourge us, so that the courting of foreign states by adopting their creed and worship must involve the courtier in ever fresh calamities. Calvin puts it more strongly still. Though God should not ascend his tribunal nor put forth his hand, though he were silent and took not on him the office of a judge, and though there were no accuser and none to plead the cause, the judgment would still be plain in their very sins; and that, he says, has far more weight in it than if the prophet had said only that God would inflict a just punishment. He finds the same manner of speaking in an older prophet, where wickedness is made to stand up against the man himself, and adds that God will heap evils on evils until they know, willing or unwilling, that what they receive is the reward due to their wickedness.
20:
Who broke the yoke is a textual crux, and they take opposite sides. Gill keeps the received reading, God breaking the yoke the nations had laid on their necks, and refers it to the deliverance from Egypt and the rescues by the judges; Wesley reads it the same way. Clarke reports that able critics put the verbs in the second person, as the Greek does, while the Latin makes it my yoke and my bonds, and he escapes by way of the Aramaic paraphrase, which has God breaking the yoke of the people from their neck. Ellicott prefers the second person outright, the sense being that they cast off all allegiance and restraint, though he allows the received text may be understood of the deliverance from bondage.

The next clause carries a second crux, and two of them change it. Ellicott follows the old versions in reading not I will not transgress but I will not serve, which paints the wilful defiance of a nation throwing off its allegiance; and if the received rendering is kept he would put the verb in the present, as expressing the same defiance. Calvin agrees on the reading, the two Hebrew letters being very similar, but rejects the exposition everyone had built on it. The prevailing gloss was I will not serve idols, and men of judgment did not see how strained it was; Calvin suspects the letter was changed for that reason.

The places of the worship they describe alike, and Henry moralises. Ellicott identifies the high hill and the green tree with the well-known high places and the named trees of an earlier prophet, notes that tree-worship exercised a wonderful power of fascination, and renders the last verb literally, laying thyself down. Clarke adds the worshippers' excuse, that elevation of that kind assisted devotion; Wesley the belief that some hidden deity lay under the shade, and the force of the verb, making haste from one tree or one idol to the next. Henry takes that restlessness for the point: they wandered from one to another like people unsettled and still unsatisfied, for those who leave God wander endlessly and a vagrant lust is insatiable.

The vine is examined closely. Ellicott gives the name literally, a Sorek vine, a word pointing first to the dark purple of the grape and then to the valley called after it, and renders the second phrase a seed of truth; he prefers hast thou changed thyself to art thou turned, and branches to plant. Keil and Delitzsch correct the figure against the older song of the vineyard: there Israel was the vineyard planted with noble vines, here Israel is the vine itself, and the word for what it became means not shoots or twigs but degenerate suckers, the article being generic, of the species of the wild vine.

What the planting was for they answer in three registers. Gill takes the noble vine of the fathers, who had the right seed of grace in them and deserved imitation by their posterity, and reports the Jewish reading that refers it to the first of them. Clarke reads it of privileges: the fullest instruction, the purest ordinances, the highest advantages, and reason would expect a suitable life, whereas the tree is deteriorated and the fruit is bad. Calvin asks why a vine at all and answers from its value, that God calls his Church his vine rather than his pasture or his field since vines are the most precious property, and so testifies how highly he prizes it; he did not deliver them from Egypt to throw aside all care of them afterwards, but that they should strike root and become a heritage precious to him. Ellicott marks the difference from the older song, where the stress fell on evil mingled with good, while here it falls on the degeneration of what God had planted.
22:
The two detergents set four of them to chemistry. Gill confesses the nitre of the ancients is unknown to us and saltpetre put in its room, and reports the Jewish guesses: alum, or a dust for cleansing the head, or an earth used on garments. Clarke insists on natron, a substance quite different from our nitre, still used in the east for washing; and he adds that vinegar poured on it effervesces strongly, which explains the proverb comparing songs sung to a heavy heart with vinegar upon natron: there is no affinity between them, and any attempt to unite them makes strife. Ellicott locates it in the Egyptian lakes that took their name from it, and corrects the second word, not soap as we know it but the potash got from the ashes of plants.

What the stain amounts to Ellicott puts by borrowing a poet: he sets beside the verse the cry of the murderer on the stage, whether all the ocean will wash the blood from his hand, and answers that the guilt was too deep-dyed in grain for outward palliatives.

The plea of innocence draws out the sharpest reading. Calvin hears hypocrites who think their pretences hide them from God, objecting, are we not God's holy people, is not this the holy seed, so that the prophets had to drive a hard wedge into a hard knot. Ellicott hears an accused criminal pleading not guilty, and answers historically: the reformation had suppressed the worship named, but the rites in the defiled valley were still practised and revived at the reformer's death, and though not that worship by name they were as evil and practically identified with it.

The wild ass they all admire and none softens. Clarke describes the fever, the mouth and nostrils opened wide for draughts of fresh air to cool the inward heat. Ellicott calls it a stronger type of passion still, startling in its boldness, with a parallel in the Roman poet's georgic; he renders the snuffing as in the desire of her heart, and notes that the male need not seek her, since she presents herself and pursues him. Calvin makes the point untamableness: shut in, bolts might stop her, but loose on hill and dale nothing will.

One short phrase gets four incompatible senses. Keil and Delitzsch keep it to the beast and make it her breeding month, refusing both the new moon as a feast and any monthly period. Ellicott makes it simply the season when the stimulus is strongest. Clarke turns it into the contrast that carries the comparison: the animal is dangerous only for a season and grows governable once satisfied, whereas these desires were never satiated, one indulgence always leading to another, so that the brute had a limit and the people none. Wesley alone hears a promise in it: though the city is now so madly bent that there is no stopping her, a time may come in her afflictions when she grows tamer and willing to receive counsel.

The unshod foot is read four ways too. Gill offers long journeys abroad for help, or a warning against going naked into captivity, or a euphemism for the adulteress putting off her shoes. Clarke takes the euphemism and extends it to the throat: she must drink no more of their libations, which only increase the appetite. Ellicott has the true husband bidding the apostate wife refrain for shame from rushing barefoot into the streets, and adds that the bare feet may belong to the worship itself, shoes being put off at the temple door. Wesley keeps it economic, that these courses will reduce her to poverty, without shoes and without the means to quench her thirst. Calvin observes what was actually asked: not a journey east or west, which might have been called irksome, but that they remain still and quiet.
26:
The thief is read four ways. Clarke puts it in the future: as the pilferer is confounded when caught in the fact, so shall they be confounded when God arrests them in their idolatries and hands them to their enemies. Ellicott takes the shame as already felt and therefore hopeful, since those who once gloried in the worship now feel as though detected in a crime, conscience having been roused again. Calvin keeps the present but drains the remorse out of it: some would render it as a threat of punishment to come, but the words as they stand say that the impiety needed no formal proof, being as public as a thief taken in the act, so that no evasion could clear them. Gill adds the qualification the figure needs, that on the Jewish reading it is the man reckoned honest who is ashamed at being found out, since those already notorious for theft feel nothing when they are caught.

The wood and the stone they distribute, and Ellicott explains why. The two words stand for images of timber and of marble, and since the second is feminine in Hebrew the grammar itself assigns the parts in the figurative parentage; he adds that the sentences read like an actual quotation from the hymns of the ritual. Clarke marks what is being claimed: to have produced and to sustain a being is the property of the true God alone, and it measures the fall that men could say it to the stock of a tree. Wesley calls it sottish stupidity to take a lifeless stock for one's maker, and Gill keeps to the plain sense, a tree, that is, an image made of one.

Calvin isolates what he thinks the detestable thing. It is not the outward act of bending the knee before a statue but the seeking of salvation from it, the honour due to God transferred; and he applies the distinction at once to the controversialists of his own day, who prostrate themselves before pictures and images and will not admit the charge of idolatry when it is brought.

The turning of the back has a sequel two of them notice. Wesley says only that they turn their faces towards their idols. Ellicott follows the turn to its end: in the time of trouble the same people who had shown their backs will seek him with outstretched hands and a cry for help, and the prophet half implies that it may be too late until chastisement has done its perfect work.

The count of the gods produces the same modern application twice over. Gill has the Lord answering his own question: what has become of the gods you chose, not the gods that made you but the ones you made yourselves. Ellicott asks it in indignant scorn, that a man should make his gods and find they cannot profit him, and notes that the Greek adds a clause about altars in the streets of the city. Wesley says they had enough of them, in imitation of heathens who by one antiquarian's count had above thirty thousand, and invites them to try whether any or all together can help. Clarke and Calvin then arrive independently at the same target. Clarke observes that among the heathen every city had its tutelary deity and that the Church of Rome has only refined the custom, giving every city its tutelary saint with a procession and worship of his own, so that not much of the old idolatry is lost; Calvin says the same of the patrons, to whom men go first and from whom they turn to God only when the superstition fails them.
29:
The challenge to plead is met alike and turned into grammar by one. Gill has them chiding and murmuring as if the Lord dealt hardly with them and they had never sinned, their case being one that would not bear opening in court. Henry calls the denial the greatest absurdity: the plea will be overruled, since they know they have all transgressed alike. Ellicott makes it the accuser's reply to a false plea, no plea being available but full confession. Calvin adds that they had gone so far as to challenge God and seek to prove him guilty, and notes that the verb takes a preposition of opposition: why should ye contend against me.

The rod having failed, the point is pressed twice over. Gill reports the rabbinic reading for vanity, of vain speaking and vain oaths, but keeps the sense that the rod was used to no purpose. Wesley makes the children the inhabitants of each city and turns correction into instruction: they were corrected without being instructed. Calvin sets beside it the older prophet's complaint that chastisement was wasted where there was no soundness from sole to crown: God tried words and scourges alike and lost his labour in both. Then the sword: Ellicott recalls the long wicked reign in which prophets rebuked at the risk of their lives and innocent blood was shed from one end of the city to the other.

Being told to see rather than hear detains three. Gill passes on the Jewish tradition that the pot of manna was brought out and shown, for their conviction. Calvin says the verb seems wrong, since attend or hear was wanted, and then defends it: they are asked not to be taught but to know, the appeal being to a fact they may see with their own eyes. Wesley gets there in a line, that they shall see the thing with their eyes because their ears are shut against it.

The two questions they answer for God. Clarke asks whether any blessing necessary for their support was ever withheld, or whether since coming out of the darkness of Egypt they had ever been brought into like circumstances, having had food for their bodies and word to enlighten their souls. Ellicott stays with the phrase, on one reading literally a darkness of Jah, the divine name expressing intensity, as elsewhere a flame of Jah means a very vehement flame.

What they answered is where the readings diverge. Ellicott renders it we rove at will rather than we are lords, Israel claiming the power to do as she likes. Clarke keeps the lordship and expands it into a manifesto: we will be our own masters, brook neither religious nor civil restraint, and regard no laws human or divine; it was this disposition, he says, that made them fall in with the whole system of idolatry. Wesley calls them words of pride and boasting.

The maid's ornaments they enjoy. Gill has the jewels laid by for a wedding day that may be tomorrow, never out of her mind, so that she can scarcely sleep for thinking how richly she will be adorned. Clarke finds the attachment greater than theirs to God, since women never forget such things and in old age look back with pleasure on the dress they wore in youth; and he dates the forgetting to the fifty-five years of one reign, in which the land was deluged with idolatry the later reform had not yet purged. Ellicott identifies the bride's article as the girdle distinguishing a wife from a maiden, treasured all her life as the marriage ring is with us, so that a woman keeps even the outward memorial while Israel forgot the husband himself. Calvin turns it into a comparison of worth: girls value such trinkets more than life, and can anything among the most precious stones compare with God?
33:
The trimming of the way is read two ways and rendered a third. Gill and Calvin take it cosmetically, the lascivious woman painting her face and dressing to excite her lovers, as the queen did who tired her head with the same word; Calvin asks why so much labour is undertaken to earn a meretricious hire. Ellicott hears irony instead: the verb is the one elsewhere rendered amend, often on the lips of men making a show of reformation, so that the question means, what is this reform that leads only to further indulgence? Clarke reports a rendering that personifies the punishment, therefore have I taught calamity thy ways: I have instructed calamity where to find thee.

Whose blood is in the skirts they divide over. Gill allows either the infants of the poor sacrificed to Moloch or the prophets who were slain, and reads the skirts as marking publicity and quantity alike, as if they had walked in it. Ellicott takes the children first and the prophets as a second possibility, and notes another reading that puts the blood on the palms of the hands. Calvin says flatly that the interpreters are mistaken, and that all of them are: what is condemned is not cruelty in general but the raging of the people against the prophets sent to heal them.

The clause about searching is a crux, and they set out its options. Clarke gives the received sense and then a rendering that turns on a dug hole: others cover blood so that it may not appear, but these shed it openly, sprinkled it on their consecrated oaks and gloried in it. Ellicott lays out the choice: either the blood was not found by a search such as men make who dig through a house wall for plunder, but was patent everywhere, or else those killed had not been caught breaking in, as a robber might be who deserved death.

The plea of innocence returns and is answered sharply. Ellicott hears her take up the accuser's own word, you speak of innocents and I too am innocent, and observes that confession might have led to forgiveness while this denial excluded it, being the token of a fatal blindness. Keil and Delitzsch explain the confidence, that a long peace and the non-fulfilment of the older threats had persuaded them the anger was turned away. Calvin calls it a brazen front, since they were proved guilty not by allegation but by glaring proof.

The gadding is a matter of policy and of lexicon. Gill has them going now one way and now another, and reports that the Latin makes the word mean how exceeding vile art thou become, one Jewish authority deriving it from a root for vileness, another from a root for going. Keil and Delitzsch make it running, and define the change of way as leaving off to seek Assyrian help in order to close with Egypt. Ellicott says the vigorous English catches the frequentative force. Calvin adds the ground of the prohibition, that seeking help from neighbours was not in itself an evil thing, but that the safety of this people was to rest elsewhere.

The last gesture they all know. Clarke identifies the hand laid on the head as the sign of deep sorrow at utter desolation, and cites the ruined woman of the old history; Wesley calls it the usual posture of mourning; Ellicott glosses the confidences as the objects trusted in. Keil and Delitzsch make the coming forth a return from Egypt with the hands beaten on the head, and extend the sentence to both powers alike, since he who broke the one will overthrow the other. Calvin sets out the calculation that made the policy look sound, the enemy twenty or thirty days away and the helper able to come at the shortest warning, and says they were greatly mistaken.
